name: Boots Soltan / star rating
lead: The Boots star rating is a UK and Ireland label that tells shoppers how much UVA protection a sunscreen gives relative to its UVB protection. For anyone trying to keep their skin looking young, even-toned and free of sun spots, the stars are a quick way to see whether a sunscreen covers the UVA rays that are associated with photoageing, alongside the SPF number that reflects UVB.

Wikipedia describes the system as a proprietary in vitro method in which five stars is the highest UVA ratio and one star the lowest [1]. Brian Diffey at Newcastle University did the original work and Boots in Nottingham developed the method, which many UK manufacturers adopted [1]. Soltan is Boots' own sunscreen range, which carries the rating on its packaging.

People using sunscreen as a looks tool, to limit tanning, pigmentation and premature lines, often look for a high star count together with a high SPF. Research has also shown how much real-world products can differ: sunscreens with the same label SPF have been found to behave differently under sunlight, and UVA performance of popular products has varied [2][3].
infobox: EU UVA seal; PA+ to PA++++ in East Asia [4]

paras: The method compares UVA to UVB protection in vitro. After revision following the Colipa UVA PF test and updated EU recommendations, samples are pre-irradiated to better reflect in-use UVA protection, and the lowest rating became three stars [1][4].

Separately, EU rules require UVA protection of at least one-third of the labelled SPF to carry the UVA seal, from European Commission Recommendation 2006/647/EC [1]. SPF itself was introduced in 1974 and EU labels cap at 50+ [1].

Asian brands, especially Japanese ones, use the PA system, based on a persistent pigment darkening reaction: PA+ corresponds to a UVA protection factor of about 2 to 4, PA++ to 4 to 8, PA+++ to above 8, and PA++++, added in 2013, to 16 or above [4]. Wikipedia notes that conventional sunscreen can block little UVA relative to its nominal SPF, which is why broad-spectrum labelling exists [4].

A 2011 study of fifteen European sunscreens with the same labelled SPF found differences in photoprotection under natural sunlight, and called for global harmonisation of photostability and UVA labelling [2]. A 2008 study assessed UVA protection in vitro of 13 popular U.S. sunscreens at a time when the U.S. had no UVA testing or labelling regulation [3]. A history review describes how sunscreen filters and regulation have evolved with understanding of UVA, UVB and visible light [5].
No studies found that evaluate the Boots star rating itself in people. Related laboratory work on UVA protection is cited above [2][3].

timeline.event: European Commission Recommendation 2006/647/EC sets the one-third UVA rule. [1]
PA++++ category added to the PA system in East Asia. [4]

card.summary: UK/Ireland star label showing a sunscreen's UVA-to-UVB protection ratio, from Boots.
card.note: Stars describe UVA ratio, not total protection; read SPF as well.

quick.overview:
The Boots star rating is a UK and Ireland label for the ratio of UVA to UVB protection in a sunscreen.

It runs up to five stars and was developed with Brian Diffey's work.
quick.mechanism: An in vitro test compares UVA to UVB protection, with pre-irradiation in the revised method.
quick.risks: Studies note labelling differences between regions and products with identical SPF.

chain: Star label shows UVA-to-UVB protection ratio
Higher UVA coverage when paired with SPF
Less UV-linked pigmentation and photoageing over time
angle.text: People who want to keep skin youthful and even-toned use the star rating to pick a sunscreen that covers UVA as well as UVB. It is a shopping aid for daily sun protection rather than a treatment.
